items.en: Grades of Severance, and Whether Restoration Is Complete
items.zh: 明罪滅階降 · 明復不復相

zh: 第二、明罪滅階降不同者，懺法既有別異，當知滅罪亦復不同。所以者何？罪有三品：一者、違無作起障道罪；二者、體性罪；三者、無明煩惱根本罪。通稱罪者，摧也。現則摧損行人功德智慧，未來之世三塗受報，則能摧折行者色心，故名為罪。一、明作法懺悔者，破違無作障道罪。二、明觀相懺者，破除體性惡業罪，故《摩訶衍論》云：「若比丘犯殺生戒，雖復懺悔，得戒清淨，障道罪滅，而殺報不滅。」此可以證前釋後，當知觀相懺悔，用功既大，能除體性之罪。三、觀無生懺悔罪滅者，破除無明一切煩惱習因之罪，此則究竟除罪源本。
en: Second, clarifying that the different grades by which offense is extinguished are not uniform: since the methods of repentance themselves differ, the extinguishing of offense likewise differs accordingly. Why is this? Offense is of three grades: first, the offense of violating the non-action precept, which obstructs the path; second, offense in its own essential nature; third, the root offense of ignorance and affliction. What is generally called "offense" means, literally, "that which crushes": in the present it crushes and diminishes the practitioner's own merit and wisdom, and in lives to come brings retribution in the three lower destinies, able to crush and break the practitioner's own body and mind — hence it is called offense.

First, as to repentance through formal procedure: this breaks the offense of violating the non-action precept that obstructs the path. Second, as to repentance through the contemplation of signs: this breaks and removes the offense of unwholesome karma in its essential nature — hence the Mahāyāna treatise says: "If a monk violates the precept against taking life, then, though he may repent and have the precept restored to purity, and the offense obstructing the path be extinguished, the karmic retribution of killing itself is not thereby extinguished." This may serve both to confirm the preceding point and to explain the one that follows: one should know that repentance through the contemplation of signs, since it requires greater effort, is able to remove offense in its essential nature as well. Third, as to the extinguishing of offense through repentance by the contemplation of no-arising: this breaks and removes the root offense of ignorance and every habituated cause of affliction — this alone is the ultimate removal of offense at its very source.

zh: 第三、明復本、不復本相者。問曰；懺悔清淨，得復本不？答曰；解者不同。有言：不復。如衣破更補，雖完，終不如不破。有言：得復。如衣不淨，更浣淨，與本無異。有言：有復，有不復。如律中所明，初二篇不復，後三篇可復。初教經所明，作羯磨懺悔，四重悉復。今言不必定爾。應當對前三種懺法還為三義：一者、復義；二者、過本義；三、增上過本義。今當借譬顯之：一者、作法懺悔，罪滅或復、不復，如冷病人服於薑桂，所患除差，身有復、不復。二者、觀相懺悔，非唯罪滅，能發禪定。此則過本。何以故？本無禪定故。如冷病人服石散等，非但冷除，亦復肥壯過本。三者、觀無生懺悔，非唯罪滅，發諸禪定，乃得成道。此為增上過本。如病服於仙藥，非直病除，乃得仙通，神變自在。此而推之，豈得一類？
en: Third, clarifying whether the mark of restoration to the original state is complete or not. Question: Once repentance brings purity, is restoration to the original state attained? Answer: Interpretations here differ. Some say: there is no restoration — like torn cloth that has been mended: though whole again, it is never quite the same as cloth that was never torn. Some say: restoration is attained — like soiled cloth that, once washed clean, is no different from what it was originally. Some say: there is both restoration and non-restoration — as explained in the Vinaya, the first two categories of offense admit no restoration, while the latter three categories can be restored; and as explained in the Sūtra of the Initial Teaching, once the formal-procedure repentance is carried out, even the four grave offenses are entirely restored. Here it is said that this need not be fixed in only one way. It should instead be matched against the three methods of repentance already given, yielding three distinct senses in turn: first, the sense of restoration; second, the sense of exceeding the original state; third, the sense of exceeding the original state to an even greater degree.

Let us illustrate this now with a comparison. First, repentance through formal procedure: the offense is extinguished, but restoration may or may not follow — like someone suffering from a cold-type illness who takes ginger and cinnamon: the ailment is cured, but the body may or may not be fully restored to its former state. Second, repentance through the contemplation of signs: not only is the offense extinguished, but dhyāna-concentration is also brought forth — this exceeds the original state, since there was originally no dhyāna-concentration at all. It is like someone suffering from a cold-type illness who takes mineral powder and the like: not only is the coldness removed, but the body also grows more robust than it originally was. Third, repentance through the contemplation of no-arising: not only is the offense extinguished and every dhyāna brought forth, but the path itself is thereby accomplished — this exceeds the original state to an even greater degree. It is like someone who, being ill, takes an elixir of immortality: not only is the illness removed, but immortal powers and self-mastered spiritual transformation are also attained. Reasoned through in this way, how could these three possibly be treated as all the same kind?

The three-grade taxonomy of offense (procedural, essential-nature, and root-ignorance) maps exactly onto the three methods of repentance, each cutting one layer deeper than the last — a structural echo of the precepts/concentration/wisdom triad running through this whole condition. The three illustrative similes (ginger and cinnamon for a cold-type illness, mineral powder for lasting vigor, an elixir for outright immortality) are Zhiyi's own way of making a fairly abstract distinction — mere restoration versus exceeding the original state versus exceeding it "to an even greater degree" — immediately intuitive.

items.en: Without Precepts, and Whether Repentance Is Always Required

zh: 問曰：有戒者可然，其無戒者云何？答曰：無戒者，當更受戒。或有因懺發戒，此如《普賢觀經》中所說。復次，若菩薩戒者，眾生世世以來，或已遇善知識，發菩提心，受菩薩戒，但於生死中顛倒造罪，妄失違犯，因今歸依三寶，重更練之，兼復懺悔清淨，用此本戒，亦發禪定。是故雖無事戒，菩提本戒或已有之。復次，如《摩訶衍論》說：「尸羅，秦言好善，好行善道，不自放逸，是名尸羅。或受戒行善，或不受戒行善，皆名尸羅。」若不受戒行善名尸羅者，既有尸羅，豈不得發諸禪三昧耶？
en: Question: This holds for one who has precepts — but what of one who lacks them? Answer: One without precepts should receive them anew. There are also cases where the precepts are brought forth through repentance itself, as described in the Samantabhadra Contemplation Sūtra.

Furthermore, as for the bodhisattva precepts: sentient beings, life after life, may already have encountered a good spiritual friend, given rise to the bodhi-mind, and received the bodhisattva precepts — only to fall, amid the confusion of birth-and-death, into committing offenses, wrongly losing or violating them. If, in the present, such a person takes refuge in the Three Jewels once more, renews this training, and also carries out repentance to purity, then, by means of this original precept, dhyāna-concentration can likewise be brought forth. Hence, even without the outward, formal precepts, the fundamental precept of bodhi may already be present.

Furthermore, as the Mahāyāna treatise says: "Śīla, in the language of the Qin dynasty, means 'fond of the good' — fond of walking the wholesome path, never given over to laxity: this is called śīla. Whether one practices what is good having received the precepts, or practices what is good without having received them, both alike are called śīla." If practicing what is good without having received the precepts can still be called śīla, then, once śīla is present, how could dhyāna and samādhi fail to be brought forth?

zh: 問曰：若爾者，何用受戒為？答曰：不然。一為助道，二定佛法外相，豈可不依？問曰：上來所說，初坐禪者必須懺悔，亦有不然？答曰：不必一向。如《妙勝定經》所明，但能直心坐禪，即是第一懺悔。若於坐中有難轉多，不得用心者，必須懺悔。
en: Question: If this is so, then what use is there in receiving the precepts at all? Answer: This does not follow. First, they assist the path; second, they establish the outward mark of the Buddhadharma — how could one not rely on them?

Question: According to what has been said above, must a beginner necessarily undergo repentance before sitting in meditation — or is this not always so? Answer: It need not always be so. As the Sūtra of the Sublime Supreme Concentration explains, simply being able to sit in meditation with a straightforward mind is itself the foremost repentance. But if, while sitting, obstacles arise in great number, such that the mind cannot be properly applied, then repentance is indeed necessary.

The closing exchange keeps the whole discussion from tipping into either extreme. Against the worry that formal ordination might seem unnecessary once śīla is redefined as simply "fond of the good": Zhiyi insists the outward precepts still matter, both as practical support and as the visible mark that distinguishes the Buddhadharma from any other path. And against the opposite worry — that this entire elaborate repentance apparatus might be a mandatory prerequisite before anyone can sit down to meditate at all — the very last line relieves the pressure: a straightforward mind sitting in meditation is already "the foremost repentance" in itself; the more elaborate methods are for when genuine obstacles actually arise, not a checklist to complete beforehand. This closes 懺悔 (repentance), and with it, all three parts of condition 1, 持戒清淨 (pure moral discipline) — the largest of the five conditions.

intro: With moral discipline fully treated, the remaining four of the five conditions move quickly by comparison.

zh: 第二、明衣食具足者。今明衣法有三種：一者、如雪山大士等學道，但畜一衣即足，以不遊人間，堪忍力成故，此上人也；二者、如迦葉等，常受頭陀法，但畜糞掃三衣，不須餘長，此是中人衣法；三者、若多寒國土及下士不堪，如來更開畜百一物等，而要應說淨作法，知量知足，若過貪求，則於道有妨。
en: Second, clarifying being complete in robes and food. Here, the practice of robes is clarified as being of three kinds: first, as with the great being of the Snowy Mountains and others who cultivate the path, keeping only a single robe is sufficient, since they do not travel among people and their power of forbearance is already accomplished — this is the practice of the superior person. Second, as with Kāśyapa and others who constantly undertake the dhutanga practices, keeping only the three robes of discarded rags, needing nothing further — this is the practice of the middling person. Third, in lands of great cold, or for the lesser practitioner who cannot bear such hardship, the Tathāgata further permits keeping a hundred and one requisite items — but this still requires the proper procedure for declaring them pure, knowing moderation and contentment; if one goes beyond this into excessive craving, it becomes an obstruction to the path.

zh: 具足食法者，食有四種：若上人大士，深山絕人，果菜隨得，趣以支命。二者、常行頭陀，受乞食法，是乞食法能破四種邪命，依正命自活，能生聖道，故名聖種。四邪命自活者：一、下口食；二、仰口食；三、四維口食；四、方口食。此是邪命之相。如舍利弗為青木女說，是中應廣分別。三者、阿蘭若，受檀越送食。四者、於僧中結淨食，有此等食，名緣具足，是名衣食具足。若無此資身因緣，則心不寧，於道有妨。
en: As for being complete in the practice of food, food is of four kinds: first, the superior person, dwelling deep in the mountains apart from other people, takes whatever fruit and vegetables can be found, simply enough to sustain life. Second, one who constantly practices the dhutanga austerities undertakes the practice of alms-begging — this practice of alms-begging is able to break the four kinds of wrong livelihood, sustaining oneself in reliance on right livelihood, able to give rise to the noble path, and is therefore called one of the noble lineages. The four kinds of wrong livelihood are: first, eating by "lowered mouth"; second, eating by "raised mouth"; third, eating by "the four intermediate-direction mouth"; fourth, eating by "the directional mouth." These are the marks of wrong livelihood, as Śāriputra explained to the woman Qingmu — this should be distinguished in full here. Third, dwelling in a forest hermitage, receiving food sent by a lay donor. Fourth, having food formally designated as pure within the saṅgha. Wherever such food is present, this is called being complete in the condition — this is what is meant by being complete in robes and food. Without this sustaining condition for the body, the mind cannot be at peace, and this becomes an obstruction to the path.

zh: 第三、得閑居靜處。閑者，不作眾事，名之為閑。無憒鬧故，名之為靜。此有三處可修禪定：一者、深山絕人之處；二者、頭陀蘭若之處，離於聚落極近二里，此放牧聲絕，無諸憒鬧；三者、遠白衣舍處，清淨伽藍之中，皆是閑居靜處也。
en: Third, obtaining a quiet, secluded dwelling place. "Quiet" means not engaged in the many affairs of ordinary life — hence it is called quiet. Being free of clamor and disturbance, it is called secluded. There are three kinds of place suitable for cultivating dhyāna-concentration here: first, a place deep in the mountains, apart from other people; second, a dhutanga hermitage, at least two li removed from any village, where the sounds of herding and grazing cannot be heard and there is no clamor of any kind; third, a place removed from the households of lay people, within a pure monastery — all of these are quiet, secluded dwelling places.

zh: 第四、息諸緣務者。緣務眾多，略說有四：一、息生活緣務，所謂不作一切有為事業；二、息人事緣務，所謂不追尋俗人、朋友、親識，斷絕往還；三、息工巧技術緣務，所謂不作世間工匠、醫方、藥呪、卜相、書數、算計等事；四、息學問緣務，所謂讀誦、聽學、義論等，悉皆棄捨，此為息諸緣務。所以者何？若多緣務，則於修定有廢，心亂難攝，不得定也。
en: Fourth, setting every worldly affair and involvement to rest. Such affairs and involvements are numerous; in brief, they may be given as four: first, setting to rest the affairs of livelihood — meaning not engaging in any conditioned occupation whatsoever; second, setting to rest personal affairs — meaning not seeking out worldly people, friends, and acquaintances, cutting off all coming and going with them; third, setting to rest the affairs of craft and technical skill — meaning not engaging in worldly trades, medicine, incantations, divination and physiognomy, calligraphy and arithmetic, calculation, and the like; fourth, setting to rest scholarly affairs — meaning reading and reciting, listening and studying, debating doctrine, and the like, all of which are to be entirely set aside. This is what is meant by setting every worldly affair and involvement to rest. Why is this? If one has many affairs and involvements, the cultivation of concentration is neglected, the mind becomes scattered and hard to gather in, and concentration cannot be attained.

zh: 第五、近善知識，有三種：一、外護善知識，經營供養，善能將護行人，不相惱亂；二者、同行善知識，共修一道，互相勸發，不相擾亂；三者、教授善知識，以內外方便禪定法門示教利喜。是則略明五緣具足。
en: Fifth, drawing near to a good spiritual friend — this is of three kinds: first, the good spiritual friend of outer protection, who manages and provides support, skillfully looking after the practitioner without causing any disturbance; second, the good spiritual friend of shared practice, who cultivates the same path together, mutually encouraging and inspiring one another without any mutual disruption; third, the good spiritual friend of instruction, who demonstrates and teaches the gates of dhyāna-concentration, both the external and internal expedient means, bringing benefit and joy. This, then, briefly clarifies being complete in the five conditions.

This closes 具五緣 (being complete in the five conditions) — the first of the twenty-five preliminary conditions' five groups — in full. Three kinds of spiritual friend recur throughout later Chinese Buddhist writing: the protector who handles practical support, the peer who practices alongside you, and the teacher who actually instructs — a useful three-way distinction, since a good relationship in one role doesn't guarantee competence in the others.

quiz.q: Offense is of three grades. Which are they?
options: the offense of violating non-action that obstructs the path; offense in its essential nature; the root offense of ignorance and affliction
the four grave, saṅgha-remainder, lower three
quiz.why: "Offense is of three grades: first, the offense of violating the non-action precept, which obstructs the path; second, offense in its own essential nature; third, the root offense of ignorance and affliction." They are three layers, not three degrees of gravity.

quiz.q: How does the text explain the word 罪 (offense)?
options: "that which crushes": it crushes merit and wisdom now and body and mind in the lower destinies later
quiz.why: "What is generally called 'offense' means, literally, 'that which crushes': in the present it crushes and diminishes the practitioner's own merit and wisdom, and in lives to come brings retribution in the three lower destinies." Covering the wholesome mind is how the text explains "hindrance."

quiz.q: The Mahāyāna treatise says a monk who kills may repent and restore the precept, yet the karmic retribution of killing is not extinguished. What does this show?
options: formal procedure only removes the path-obstructing offense; sign-contemplation, requiring greater effort, removes the essential-nature offense
quiz.why: "First, as to repentance through formal procedure: this breaks the offense of violating the non-action precept that obstructs the path ... one should know that repentance through the contemplation of signs, since it requires greater effort, is able to remove offense in its essential nature as well." The path-obstructing offense is removed, so repentance does work; the retribution remaining shows the need for a deeper method.

quiz.q: Which grade of offense does repentance by contemplating no-arising remove?
options: the path-obstructing offense of violating non-action
the offense of ignorance and every habituated cause of affliction — removing offense at its very source
quiz.why: "As to the extinguishing of offense through repentance by the contemplation of no-arising: this breaks and removes the root offense of ignorance and every habituated cause of affliction — this alone is the ultimate removal of offense at its very source."

quiz.q: On whether purity through repentance restores the original state, which three earlier views does the text list?
options: restoration takes three, seven, or ten years
all yes; all no; the teacher decides
no, like mended cloth; yes, like washed cloth; partly — the first two categories cannot be restored, the latter three can
quiz.why: "Some say: there is no restoration — like torn cloth that has been mended ... Some say: restoration is attained — like soiled cloth that, once washed clean, is no different ... Some say: there is both restoration and non-restoration — as explained in the Vinaya, the first two categories of offense admit no restoration, while the latter three categories can be restored." Zhiyi himself says it need not be fixed.

quiz.q: The text matches three medicinal similes to the three methods. Which pairing is correct?
options: procedure: elixir; signs: ginger; no-arising: mineral powder
procedure: mineral; signs: elixir; no-arising: ginger
procedure: ginger and cinnamon, may or may not restore; signs: mineral powder, more robust than before; no-arising: elixir, immortal powers, exceeding even further
quiz.why: Formal procedure is "like someone suffering from a cold-type illness who takes ginger and cinnamon"; sign-contemplation like one who "takes mineral powder ... the body also grows more robust than it originally was"; no-arising like one who "takes an elixir of immortality ... immortal powers ... are also attained." They are restoration, exceeding, and exceeding to a greater degree.

quiz.q: Why is sign-contemplation repentance said to "exceed the original state"?
options: not only is the offense extinguished, but dhyāna is brought forth, which was not there originally
because precepts are no longer needed
quiz.why: "Not only is the offense extinguished, but dhyāna-concentration is also brought forth — this exceeds the original state, since there was originally no dhyāna-concentration at all." Accomplishing the path belongs to no-arising repentance.

quiz.q: Asked about one who lacks precepts, how does the text answer?
options: they can only recite the Buddha's name
they should receive them anew; some receive them through repentance; bodhisattva precepts may already exist from past lives and, renewed with repentance, can bring forth dhyāna
quiz.why: "One without precepts should receive them anew. There are also cases where the precepts are brought forth through repentance itself ... Hence, even without the outward, formal precepts, the fundamental precept of bodhi may already be present."

quiz.q: If practicing good without precepts is also śīla, why receive the precepts at all?
options: first, they assist the path; second, they establish the outward mark of the Buddhadharma
quiz.why: "Question: If this is so, then what use is there in receiving the precepts at all? Answer: This does not follow. First, they assist the path; second, they establish the outward mark of the Buddhadharma — how could one not rely on them?"

quiz.q: Must a beginner always repent before sitting in meditation? What sūtra does the text cite?
options: a favorable sign must first be seen
always seven days of repentance first
not always; the Sublime Supreme Concentration Sūtra says sitting with a straightforward mind is the foremost repentance; repent when obstacles multiply
quiz.why: "It need not always be so. As the Sūtra of the Sublime Supreme Concentration explains, simply being able to sit in meditation with a straightforward mind is itself the foremost repentance. But if, while sitting, obstacles arise in great number ... then repentance is indeed necessary."

quiz.q: Which correctly describes the three kinds of robe practice?
options: the superior keep a single robe; the middling, like Kāśyapa, three robes of rags; in cold lands or for the lesser, a hundred and one items are permitted
everyone may keep a hundred and one items
quiz.why: "First, as with the great being of the Snowy Mountains ... keeping only a single robe is sufficient ... Second, as with Kāśyapa ... keeping only the three robes of discarded rags ... Third, in lands of great cold, or for the lesser practitioner ... the Tathāgata further permits keeping a hundred and one requisite items."

quiz.q: Alms-begging breaks the four kinds of wrong livelihood. Which are they?
options: lowered mouth, raised mouth, four-intermediate-direction mouth, directional mouth
quiz.why: "The four kinds of wrong livelihood are: first, eating by 'lowered mouth'; second, eating by 'raised mouth'; third, eating by 'the four intermediate-direction mouth'; fourth, eating by 'the directional mouth.'"

quiz.q: Food is of four kinds. Which of the following is among them?
options: dwelling in a forest hermitage and receiving food sent by a lay donor
quiz.why: The four are fruit and vegetables in the deep mountains, alms-begging, "third, dwelling in a forest hermitage, receiving food sent by a lay donor," and food designated as pure within the saṅgha. The text says that without this support the mind cannot be at peace; it does not advocate fasting.

quiz.q: Of the three quiet places for cultivating dhyāna, how far must the second, a dhutanga hermitage, be from a village?
options: at least two li, where the sounds of herding cannot be heard
any distance, as long as it is quiet
quiz.why: "Second, a dhutanga hermitage, at least two li removed from any village, where the sounds of herding and grazing cannot be heard and there is no clamor of any kind." The others are the deep mountains and a pure monastery removed from lay households.

quiz.q: Of the four affairs to set to rest, what is the fourth, scholarly affairs?
options: not engaging in trades, medicine, divination
not engaging in any conditioned occupation
not seeking out worldly friends and acquaintances
reading and reciting, listening and studying, debating doctrine — all set aside
quiz.why: "Fourth, setting to rest scholarly affairs — meaning reading and reciting, listening and studying, debating doctrine, and the like, all of which are to be entirely set aside." Trades and divination are the third, friends the second, and occupations the first.

quiz.q: What are the three kinds of good spiritual friend?
options: of outer protection, of shared practice, of instruction
quiz.why: "First, the good spiritual friend of outer protection, who manages and provides support ...; second, the good spiritual friend of shared practice, who cultivates the same path together ...; third, the good spiritual friend of instruction, who demonstrates and teaches the gates of dhyāna-concentration."
